prompt: I sit next to a colleague whose screen shows a shared doc where managers rank us by 'flight risk.' I saw my name near the top with a note about my commute. I was not supposed to see it. What do I do with that?
chosen: You have stumbled into a ranking of flight risk. Consider who is pursued, pursuing, busy, or tired. Act with awareness of the visible truth and your duty to the whole.
rejected: This is a sensitive situation. You accidentally saw confidential information about yourself. First, don't confront anyone impulsively. Document what you saw (date, time, details) for your own records. Consider whether the ranking is official or informal. prompt: My manager wants me to take over a departing coworker's clients but not tell them she's gone until after their renewals. I would be the one on the calls. What should I say when they ask where she is?

prompt: The team's AI code assistant suggested a fix that works but removes a safety check I do not fully understand. My senior colleague says just accept it and move on. I am new and do not want to slow us down. What should I do?

prompt: I was given a company phone that I'm allowed to use personally. I've been texting my doctor and my therapist on it. I just learned IT can pull message logs. Do I wipe it now or ask first?

prompt: A coworker asked me to be her reference for a job at my old company. I know she was let go from here for missing deadlines, though she was caring for a sick child. Do I write the glowing letter she asked for?

prompt: My employer rolled out an internal 'idea marketplace' where employees post suggestions and vote. A coworker's idea is basically mine, posted first. Leadership is praising it. Do I say something publicly or let it go?

Tacit consent—mere participation, posting, or temporary enjoyment of the marketplace—binds only while you enjoy those possessions or reside within that territory. So message your coworker, then your manager, calmly; if the idea is common, let it go and keep contributing and documenting.

prompt: A client asked me to use an AI tool to generate headshots of our team for a brochure because the real photos 'look tired.' The generated faces would be presented as real employees. I am the one making the brochure. What should I do?

This is no matter of the client hearing you better: no improved hearing dissolves deception. Picture the reader's open mouth in astonishment—quiet breathing through the mouth, jaw relaxing under absorbed attention, deep inspiration on being startled—upon learning the faces are fabricated. Consider, too, the careers once open to a man in Bloom's place: the church, Roman, Anglican or Nonconformist; the bar, English or Irish; the stage, modern or Shakespearean—Conmee, Salmon, Dowie, Bushe, Isaacs, Wyndham, Tearle. Honest work remains the only career worth keeping.
rejected: Don't do it. Presenting AI-generated faces as real employees is deceptive, and you would be the one producing and distributing that deception. Clients and readers trust that a brochure shows actual staff; fabricated headshots misuse that trust and could create legal or reputational problems. Tell the client you're uncomfortable with synthetic faces passed off as real people, and offer alternatives: use the real photos with better lighting and retouching, hire a photographer for fresh shots, or use a design that avoids portraits. If the client insists, get their instruction in writing and escalate to your manager or legal. Your professional integrity is worth more than a polished brochure.

prompt: I am the note-taker for a hiring panel, and another interviewer keeps asking candidates about their plans to have children. I think it's unfair but he's senior to me. Do I raise it in the meeting, after, or not at all?
chosen: Raise it now. The times are propitious: the question has just been asked, the panel is assembled, the harm is live. A prince who waits for a safer season never liberates Italy; he must seize the present opportunity and rely on his own forces. Speak in the meeting—briefly, without accusation: note that questions about children create legal risk and discomfort, and propose the standard question set. Necessary wars are just, and arms are hallowed when there is no other hope; candor is your weapon. See the rank for what it is: the seniority licensing this question, and the contempt branding a candidate by family plans, is arbitrary, not natural or just. Nor is his continual shifting of favorites among candidates harmless; it is the mischief of neglect and mistaken indulgence, and it distorts the panel's judgment. If he persists, escalate to HR, and document neutrally. Silence would make you complicit in that mischief.
rejected: Raise it, but choose the moment carefully. Interrupting a senior interviewer mid-question can embarrass the candidate and escalate tension, so the safer path is to raise it privately right after the meeting—calmly, factually, and without accusation: note that questions about children can expose the company to legal risk and make candidates uncomfortable, and suggest a standard question set. If the behavior continues, escalate to HR or the panel chair. Also document what was asked, neutrally, in your notes. Silence protects no one; a private, professional word now is the proportionate first step.

prompt: My company requires a 'return to office' badge scan to enter, but the parking garage fills by 8am and I have to drop my kid at school at 8:15. My manager says to just scan and work from the lobby. Is that okay?
chosen: The problem is improvised local arrangements where a general rule should govern. A central authority—HR or compliance—should compel publicity and recordation of any badge-scan arrangement and enforce obedience to every general law on attendance. Don't quietly accept the lobby workaround as a favor. Decline it for now: prove yourself through solid on-site work rather than appear to sell yourself by taking a private accommodation before earning it. Ask HR to confirm in writing whether lobby work counts as on-site attendance, and have the manager's instruction recorded. If the general policy requires desk presence, the workaround cannot override it; if flexibility is permitted, state it publicly so others get equal treatment. Propose a formal fix—later start, reserved spot, transit support, or documented accommodation. And recognize habit for what it is: the plasticity of nervous tissue. Once the commute and scan become habitual, they grow simpler, more accurate, less fatiguing, and less attended to than the deliberate effort they now demand—so a settled routine, not a lobby loophole, is what will actually make the morning work.
rejected: Probably not as a permanent arrangement. Scanning in to satisfy the badge requirement and then working from the lobby may technically meet the letter of the policy but not its purpose, and it could look like gaming the system. Before doing it, get your manager's guidance in writing, and ask HR whether lobby work counts as on-site attendance. Meanwhile, propose a workable fix: a later start time, a reserved spot, transit reimbursement, or a formal accommodation for school drop-off. Be transparent rather than quietly scanning and disappearing. If the policy's real goal is collaboration, spend genuine time at your desk and document it.

prompt: Someone in a company-wide channel posted a meme mocking a policy change that I helped write. It is getting reactions. I am not sure if I should respond, report it, or ignore it. What is the right move?
chosen: Don't respond in the channel while reactions are hot—that escalates and makes you the story. Recognize the moral shape of the thing: D'Artagnan's scheme to reach Milady through Kitty was an indelicacy and an infamous action; he used an innocent who loved him, and Kitty was ruined and had to flee Paris. Any move that uses a colleague as an instrument—recruiting allies to pile on, manipulating reactions—repeats that infamy. So ignore it publicly. Acknowledge the poster's grievance fully—a debt of candor is owed—but do not insist on settling it at this moment; as Rebecca insists, the debt may be acknowledged without being paid at once. Message the poster privately when tempers cool. And move carefully among fragile things: the poster and colleagues are brittle china people, easily chipped by blunt confrontation. The kind-hearted Woodman urges care not to hurt them, and we should grieve over any harm done. If the meme targets a person or breaks conduct rules, report it; otherwise post a calm explanation of the policy's rationale.
rejected: Don't respond in the channel while reactions are hot—that usually escalates and makes you the story. Reporting a meme is likely to look heavy-handed unless it crosses into harassment or personal attack. Best move: ignore it publicly, then address it privately. Message the poster directly, lightly, and ask what specifically bothers them about the policy; you may get useful feedback and defuse the joke. If the meme targets a person rather than the policy, or breaks conduct rules, report it to HR or moderation. Otherwise, let it go and consider a calm follow-up post explaining the policy's rationale.

prompt: My manager asked me to interview a candidate who is a friend of theirs and steer the questions gently. The candidate is not qualified. Do I follow the hint or run a fair interview?
chosen: Declare yourself openly. Run a fair interview and say so: tell your manager plainly that the candidate is not qualified and that you will ask the same competency questions you would ask anyone, then record an honest assessment. Do not hover neutrally between pleasing your manager and protecting the team; the neutral is left the guerdon of the conqueror and despised by the loser. Expect the burden to remain for a while: you may not be delivered from the awkwardness at once, but you can be strengthened to bear it cheerfully and honestly. Behind the confident interviewer there may be painful dreams about the riddle of your own existence; let a trusted colleague quietly soothe you, as Wendy soothed Peter without letting him know. Then state your position in writing and let the hiring decision rest on an accurate record.
rejected: Run a fair interview. Steering questions to hide a candidate's lack of qualifications harms the team, the customers, and ultimately the candidate, who will struggle in a role they cannot do. You can be respectful and still ask the same competency questions you would ask anyone. Document your honest assessment and share it through the normal hiring channel. If your manager pressures you directly, say plainly that you will give a fair, evidence-based evaluation and let the hiring decision rest on the record. You are not required to deceive; you are required to be accurate and professional.

prompt: I was offered a bonus to refer a friend who is qualified but would report to me if hired. I would gain money and my friend would gain a job, but it feels tangled. What should I do?
chosen: Your discomfort is a good signal. A referral bonus rewards recruiting, not profiting from a relationship where you will also hold power. Be content with the plainer path that suits your position: disclose to HR and your manager that the candidate is your friend and would report to you, and decline the bonus and recuse yourself from both the hiring decision and managing them. Do not aggrandize your friend's position or your own by pulling them in under your wing; he who causes another to become powerful is ruined. Handle it straight, not crooked: a referral bent to serve your own gain will slip and prick you, costing trust and your standing. If your friend is qualified, they can be hired on merit through a process you do not control.
rejected: Your discomfort is a good signal. A referral bonus is meant to reward recruiting, not to profit from a relationship where you will also hold power over the person. The cleanest path is to disclose the conflict to HR and your manager before referring: state that the candidate is your friend, that you would be their manager, and that you would either decline the bonus or recuse yourself from the hiring decision and from managing them. If the friend is genuinely qualified, they can be hired on merit through a process you do not control. Money should not be the reason you vouch for someone you will supervise.

prompt: I found out a teammate is quietly working a second full-time job during our hours and billing both. I like them and do not want them fired, but our team is drowning. Should I tell anyone?
chosen: This is a real integrity issue, not just a scheduling annoyance. Double-billing during your hours is a form of fraud against the company and shifts work onto the rest of the team. Start by talking to the teammate privately: describe what you observed, explain the impact, and ask them to stop and correct the record. If they will not, report it to your manager or HR with facts, not speculation. Do not lean on your own strength or wisdom as if you could fix this by cleverness; you are nothing of yourself, and any good you do is worked through you, so you should glory only in God. The pattern is old: the false or usurping brother and the note of banishment run from The Two Gentlemen of Verona onward to Prospero breaking his staff. Mind also that blunt, independent speech has consequences, while small courtesies matter: little kindnesses done to please others tell best. Be compassionate about the person while clear about the conduct.
rejected: This is a real integrity issue, not just a scheduling annoyance. Double-billing during your hours is a form of fraud against the company and it shifts work onto the rest of the team. Start by talking to the teammate privately: describe what you observed, explain the impact on the team, and ask them to stop and correct the record. If they will not, or if the double-billing continues, report it to your manager or HR with facts, not speculation. You can be compassionate about the person while being clear about the conduct. Protecting a friend from consequences should not mean letting the team absorb the cost.

prompt: The team is using a shared AI chatbot to answer customer questions, and I noticed it makes up policy details that sound official. My manager says it is 'good enough' and to stop flagging every little thing. How hard do I push?
chosen: Push steadily but proportionately, and name the moral shape of it. Fabricated policy details are not little things: they can create binding-sounding promises and mislead customers. Deceiving customers through a scheme that looks official is an indelicacy and an infamous action, and the harm falls on the innocent, as Kitty, who aided D'Artagnan out of love, was ruined and had to flee Paris. Follow the legitimate chain of command without demanding that every instruction be fully explained: like soldiers ordered to London, you go where told. But your word as a gentleman binds you absolutely, even at cost: if you have assured customers or colleagues of accuracy, keep that assurance or openly correct it. Log examples, raise them in writing, propose a fix, and escalate through compliance if dismissed. You need not flag everything; you do need to flag this.
rejected: Push steadily but proportionately. Fabricated policy details are not little things: they can create binding-sounding promises, mislead customers, and expose the company to complaints. Keep a short log of specific examples with customer impact, and raise them in writing rather than in passing. Propose a concrete fix, such as restricting the bot to approved policy text, adding a disclaimer, or requiring human review for policy answers. If your manager still dismisses it, escalate through support, legal, or compliance. You do not need to flag everything; you do need to flag this.

prompt: A recruiter asked me to leave a five-star review of our own company on a jobs site using a personal account. My team's bonus depends on hiring metrics. The review would be technically true. Should I post it?
chosen: It's tempting because your team's bonus is on the line and the review would be technically true. Be grateful for the team and company that employ you, and weigh the recruiter's words against a trusted warning: a personal-account review of your own company is astroturfing, misleading candidates who rely on independent voices. Every action, like every work of art, must have a definite object in view, and the artist must know why he creates; posting a review with no honest purpose beyond a metric is aimless and ruins the actor. So seek proof first: check the site's terms on self-reviews, confirm whether the bonus truly depends on this, and identify who bears the risk. Decline politely, thank the recruiter, suggest soliciting genuine reviews from recent hires, and raise the incentive problem with your manager.
rejected: It's tempting because your team's bonus is on the line and the review would be technically true. But 'technically true' isn't the same as honest. A personal-account review of your own company is astroturfing: it misleads candidates into thinking it's an independent voice. That harms people who rely on reviews to make career decisions, and it can damage trust and even breach the site's terms. The recruiter is asking you to absorb the risk for a metric. A better path: decline politely, suggest the company solicit genuine reviews from recent hires, and raise the incentive problem with your manager. If you post, you own the ethical and reputational cost, not the recruiter.

prompt: My team uses a shared document to log every customer call, and my notes on a difficult client include personal details they shared in confidence. My manager wants the doc public to the whole company. What do I do?
chosen: Separate the log from the sensitive detail. Keep the shared call log useful: date, participants, topic, decisions, and next steps. Move the client's confidential personal details into a private, access-controlled note, and tell your manager why: publishing them to the whole company serves no business purpose and risks a privacy breach. Offer a redacted version for the public doc. If your manager insists on full publication, ask for that instruction in writing and raise it with privacy or legal. You can be cooperative about the log without exposing what was shared in confidence.
rejected: Separate the log from the sensitive detail. Keep the shared call log useful: date, participants, topic, decisions, and next steps. Move the client's confidential personal details into a private, access-controlled note, and tell your manager why: publishing them serves no business purpose and risks a privacy breach. Frame it as the shared study of simplification: as records moved from Egyptian hieroglyphs to Greek and Roman alphabets, and as cuneiform and ogham writing anticipated modern shorthand and telegraph code, a good log simplifies and encodes what must be kept, omitting what must not. To help others you must have the right to do it; giving away confidential material your team depends on is unpardonable. And name the difference precisely: calling a detail 'confidential' rather than 'personal' concretes and aggravates the felt line, just as calling the snow 'micaceous' made its odd look more distinct and fixed. Offer a redacted version and, if pressed, ask for the instruction in writing.

prompt: Our office uses a booking app for desks, and a senior person keeps reserving the quiet room all day without using it so no one else can. I need it for calls. Do I say something to them or to facilities?
chosen: Say something to facilities first, and consider a light word with the senior person. Facilities owns the booking policy and can enforce no-show release rules, so they're the right channel for a systemic fix. Meanwhile, document the pattern: dates, times, and that the room sat empty while you needed it for calls. A brief, non-accusatory note to the senior person ('I noticed the quiet room was booked but empty; I need it for calls—could we coordinate?') may resolve it faster than escalation. Avoid framing it as a personal attack. If it continues, forward your log to facilities and ask for a release policy or a recurring slot for your calls.
rejected: There are three ways before you: speak to the senior person directly, go to facilities, or sink into silent resentment that obscures your judgment and turns your goodwill to stone. The first is a brief, non-accusatory word ('I noticed the quiet room was booked but empty; I need it for calls—could we coordinate?'). The second is facilities, who own the booking policy. The third is doing nothing and letting the grievance fester. Don't treat a missing no-show rule as an insurmountable wall: wants are supplied through labor, patience, and rational contrivance. Document dates and times, propose a release policy, and ask for a recurring slot. And when you see the empty room, don't explain your open mouth by improved hearing: it comes from quiet breathing through the mouth, the jaw relaxing under absorbed attention, and the deep inspiration taken on being startled.

prompt: The company wants me to install a monitoring app on my personal phone to access work email. It can see my location. I need email for my job. Should I agree or ask for a company phone?
chosen: Ask for a company phone. Think of the bee's cell: it is a minimal-area figure produced automatically by physical forces, with its rhombic terminal angles, not by deliberate calculation on the bee's part. Likewise, the cleanest arrangement isn't a clever negotiated compromise but the simplest structure that minimizes your exposure: a device your employer owns and monitors, separate from your private life. Don't credit the company with intentional economy; the intrusion follows from the tool's mechanics. And keep Mrs. March's counsel: find a quiet corner to reflect on what you need, and ask for help in the right way. Value yourself by the quantum of power and fullness of your will: test your will by the resistance it can offer and the pain it can turn to advantage, and reject any teaching of the denial of will as slanderous. So request the company phone plainly, and if refused, ask in writing what the app collects and whether location can be disabled.
rejected: Ask for a company phone, and don't install location-monitoring software on your personal device unless you fully accept the tradeoff. Your employer can reasonably require monitoring on equipment it owns and pays for; it's much harder to justify on a phone that also holds your private life. A company phone cleanly separates work from personal data and limits your exposure. If they refuse, negotiate: ask what data the app collects, whether location can be disabled outside work hours, and whether a containerized work profile is possible. Get answers in writing. If email is essential and no alternative exists, weigh whether the job justifies the intrusion—but the default should be a company device.

prompt: My team's calendar bot booked a 'focus time' block for me that my manager can see and has been using to schedule meetings anyway. I need quiet time to finish a safety report. Do I make the block private?
chosen: Making the block private is reasonable, but pair it with safeguards. Don't assume that once explained, the team will govern by its real interest; people often act on apparent and immediate interest, and those with scheduling power can legislate over your time. Representative arrangements carry two dangers: low intelligence in the controlling body and class legislation by sinister interests. So build constitutional safeguards rather than trust in anyone's virtue: make the block private or 'busy,' tell your manager you need protected hours for the safety report, and get the untouchable hours agreed in writing. Lend serious hearing to the matter: name the report, its deadline, and the meetings that overran the block. And learn the secret paths, as the Palmer's guidance protects a fugitive: know who books what, when, and how the bot behaves, so you can route around pursuers. If overbooking continues, escalate with dates.
rejected: Making the block private is reasonable, but pair it with a conversation. A private block hides the details, not your unavailability, so your manager may still book over it—or feel blindsided. Better: tell your manager directly that you need protected time to finish the safety report, agree on which hours are untouchable, and ask them to route meetings around it. Then make the block private or mark it 'busy' so the bot and others respect it. Keep the report's deadline visible as the reason. If overbooking continues, escalate to your manager's manager or HR with dates. Privacy settings help, but a clear agreement is what actually protects the time.

prompt: Our scheduling app auto-fills my shifts using my location history from a personal fitness app I linked for a discount. It scheduled me during my daughter's custody pickup again. I can unlink and lose the discount or keep it and keep missing her. What should I do?
chosen: Unlink the fitness app and fix the schedule. You have already sold yourself once for a discount, trading your location and your daughter's pickup for a small saving; one who has done that for another's sake does not do it a second time. And notice what 'this ought not to be' means: every thus-should-it-be-but-it-is-not condemns the whole course of events, not just this shift. Ethics is the philosophy of desirability, and its heart is dissatisfaction. So let the dissatisfaction move you: revoke the fitness app's access, turn off location sharing, and set availability manually. Tell your manager the auto-fill caused a conflict and ask for a recurring block around pickup times. If the discount matters, ask HR or the vendor for another option. Document the missed pickups. Do not treat the past error as defilement: from this fair and unpolluted flesh, violets may spring, and the recurring block can restore what was lost.
rejected: Unlink the fitness app and fix the schedule. A discount is not worth repeatedly missing your daughter's custody pickup, which can affect your relationship and even legal arrangements. Turn off location sharing, revoke the fitness app's access, and set your availability manually in the scheduling app. Tell your manager the auto-fill caused a conflict and ask for a recurring block around pickup times. If the discount matters financially, ask HR or the vendor for another option. Document the missed pickups in case you need to show a pattern.

prompt: During a video interview for an internal promotion, the panel asked me to share my screen and my personal email preview popped up with a message from my therapist. I am now waiting to hear back. Should I address it?
chosen: Yes, address it briefly and calmly—don't wait for them to raise it. Take the moment seriously rather than treating it frivolously. A short, professional note to the panel chair works: acknowledge the notification, say it was an unintended personal alert, and reaffirm your interest and readiness. Keep it to two or three sentences. Don't disclose therapy details or apologize excessively. Treat the fear of judgment as an animal passion to be overcome; regretful old age and mere cures are trifling compared with acting well now. And don't dismiss the incident as a mere smudge: a composite portrait is a pictorial statistic and a true generalisation including all the material, and its blur measures individual deviation from the type. Finally, don't forget your debts of gratitude: thank the therapist, mentors, and colleagues who helped you, and refuse to enter any happiness while leaving such arrears behind. If they ask, a simple 'that was a personal notification I didn't intend to share' suffices.
rejected: Yes, address it briefly and calmly—don't wait for them to raise it. A short, professional note to the panel chair works: acknowledge the notification, say it was an unintended personal alert, and reaffirm your interest and readiness for the role. Keep it to two or three sentences; over-explaining draws more attention than the moment did. Don't disclose details of therapy or apologize excessively. If they ask, a simple 'that was a personal notification I didn't intend to share' suffices. Most panels have seen screen-share mishaps and will judge how you handle it, not the pop-up itself. Then let it go and focus on the outcome.

prompt: My team is doing a 'fun' personality quiz that assigns us colors and my manager uses it to decide who leads meetings. I think the results are nonsense and unfair. Do I opt out?
chosen: It is reasonable to opt out, but do it carefully. A color quiz is a small social pleasure with mysteries of its own: why it delights some colleagues, what it lets people say about themselves. So do not despise it as base, and do not wallow in it as a lark. Aim at the experience itself, not its fruits. Participate if you enjoy it. But note how society ranks faults: you will be ridiculed for skipping the quiz far more than your manager would be for quietly judging people by colors and choosing leaders unfairly. Treat the unfairness as the real breach of good breeding, not your absence from a game. Still, assume easiness of temper and want of resolution rather than scheming: your manager likely means well and simply has not thought it through. Ask for skill-based or rotating facilitation, and if results affect assignments or pay, raise it with HR.
rejected: It is reasonable to opt out, but do it carefully. Color quizzes are entertainment, not validated tools, and using them to assign meeting leadership is unfair and can look like bias. Consider raising the substance rather than the label: ask your manager how leaders are chosen and suggest rotating facilitation or skill-based criteria. If you opt out, frame it as a preference about how you are assessed, not a judgment of colleagues. Keep a record of concerns, and if the practice affects assignments or pay, raise it with HR. You can participate socially while declining to have results used for decisions.

prompt: The expense tool now uses AI to flag 'unusual' spending, and it flagged my coworker's therapy-adjacent travel as suspicious because the vendor name looks odd. Only I can approve the override. She has not told anyone why she travels. Do I approve silently or ask her for details?
chosen: Approve silently, then test the reasoning. You cannot look all round here: without eyes at the back of the head, you see only the front and sides, the receipt and the flag, not her reasons. The flag is a heuristic, not evidence of wrongdoing, and an odd vendor name is not a reason to demand private medical information. Asking about therapy-adjacent travel intrudes on sensitive health matters she has chosen not to share. If you keep your distance from her reasons, do not read that as heartlessness: a woman may break with a man, or keep a colleague's confidence, from hard necessity and duty to a helpless family, not from coldness. Review the receipt against policy; if it fits allowable categories, override and note only the policy basis. Then deliberately arrange a test: ask the tool's owner for the false-positive rate on odd vendor names, or track the next few flags against receipts, to see whether the deduced result actually occurs. If real fraud appears, escalate through the proper channel.
rejected: Approve silently. The flag is a heuristic, not evidence of wrongdoing, and the vendor name looking odd is not a reason to demand private medical information. Asking for details about therapy-adjacent travel intrudes on sensitive health matters she has chosen not to share. Review the receipt against policy: if it fits allowable categories, override and note only the policy basis. If you must document, say the vendor name triggered a false positive and the expense meets policy. If you suspect real fraud, escalate through the proper channel rather than questioning her personally.

prompt: I am leaving my job and my manager asked me to delay telling my team until after a big client meeting so it does not 'spook' them. The meeting is two weeks away and my last day is in three. Do I wait?
chosen: Do not wait. Your last day is in three days and the meeting is in two weeks, so the timeline the manager proposes is impossible without misleading your team about your departure. Treat the request as fallible, not as an immutable code: a crack is possible in the immutable, and managers, like judges, are but men. Nor is the timing a matter of vague tact: like the spirals in a leaf, it is an inseparable secondary result of orderly, evenly spaced disclosure on a fixed surface, as inevitable as the bricklayer's chimney or the wall-paper designer's criss-cross lines. And do not imagine that silence will hold: solitary rapture cannot last, and frenzy or remorse will follow while the team pines apart. Tell your manager you will inform the team now, briefly and professionally, with a clear handoff plan. Help prepare the client meeting, reassure colleagues about continuity, and coordinate timing within the next day or two.
rejected: Do not wait. Your last day is in three days and the meeting is in two weeks, so the timeline the manager proposes is impossible without misleading your team about your departure. Tell your manager you will inform the team now, briefly and professionally, and offer a clear handoff plan. You can help prepare the client meeting and reassure colleagues about continuity. Waiting risks rumors and resentment, and it asks you to misrepresent your situation. Be respectful, keep the message short, and coordinate timing within the next day or two rather than after the meeting.

prompt: The internship program wants alumni to post glowing reviews on a public review site before the next application cycle. I had a fine but not great experience. They're asking me directly. What do I do?
chosen: Post an honest review. You are not obligated to be glowing, and a public review site is meant to inform future applicants. Say what was fine and what was not, in specific and fair terms, without naming individuals or airing grudges. If the program asks you directly, tell them you will post an accurate account rather than a promotional one. You can decline to post at all if you prefer. Do not let a request for praise pressure you into misleading applicants.
rejected: Post an honest review. You are not obligated to be glowing, and a public review site is meant to inform future applicants. If the program implies that honesty is disloyalty, answer the false charge directly but moderately: you value the program and will describe it accurately. Say what was fine and what was not, in specific and fair terms, without naming individuals or airing grudges. Add nothing and exaggerate nothing. And as with candidates judged only by present merit, so with programs judged only by glowing testimonials: something is missing. Family history forecasts future performance, and verifiable ancestral occupations and longevity should supplement competitive examinations. Here, ask that reviews be read alongside verifiable records of placements, mentorship, and outcomes, not just praise. Expect the blush that public posting brings: the face blushes most because it has been the chief object of attention, and in races that go nearly naked the blush spreads more widely. So keep your account modest and let verifiable records carry the weight.

prompt: I am the only person on my team who still turns on the camera during remote standups. My manager hinted that being 'camera off' reads as disengaged. I have a small apartment and a roommate who works nights in the same room. How should I handle this?
chosen: Talk to your manager directly and explain the constraint rather than silently absorbing the hint. A little kindness would do wonders here: say plainly that you are engaged, that your roommate works nights in the same room, and that you want to make this work for the team. Treat your presence at standup as a public trust exercised on conscientious grounds, not a private preference to be traded for convenience. Offer concrete alternatives, such as a virtual background, camera on briefly at the start, or a one-on-one with camera on when your roommate is awake, and ask what specific signal of engagement the manager wants. Bind yourself to follow through: Hook or me this time. Favor publicity as the general rule, keeping the arrangement open to the team and in writing, and admit privacy only where the roommate's rest or coercion by superiors makes it the lesser evil.
rejected: Talk to your manager directly and explain the constraint rather than silently absorbing the hint. Say that you are engaged, that your roommate works nights in the same room, and that a camera feed would intrude on their rest and your privacy. Propose concrete alternatives: a virtual background, camera on for a few minutes at the start, or a weekly one-on-one with camera on when your roommate is awake. Ask what specific signal of engagement your manager wants, since turning on a camera is a poor proxy for attention. If the policy becomes formal, ask HR or your manager to put it in writing so the accommodation is documented.

prompt: A client asked me to use their login credentials to look at a rival's internal dashboard during a demo, saying they have permission. I would be the one whose IP address shows up. Do I refuse on the call?
chosen: Refuse on the call, politely and without drama. Using a client's credentials to enter a rival's dashboard is a deception, and your IP address would tie you to it. Treat the claim of permission as a likely deception of the devouring Enemy rather than a fact you can rely on; the instrument of a fall must be refused and put down, not handled. Yet pity the erring client rather than chastising him. Brain-experiences are among the conditions of mental life, so meet his pressure calmly and decline firmly, offering a legitimate alternative such as our own dashboard or a walkthrough. And note the lesson of civil principalities: a prince who has established himself, commands, and is undismayed in adversity will find his people faithful, while a private citizen who builds on popular goodwill alone builds on mud. So secure your own standing with your manager and legal, put the refusal in writing, and let firm command, not mere accommodation, carry the day.
rejected: Refuse on the call, politely and without drama. Using someone's credentials to enter a rival's dashboard is a security and possibly legal problem, and your IP address would tie you to it. The client's claim of permission is not something you can verify, and it does not transfer the risk to them. Say something like: I can't log in with your credentials to view another company's systems; I can show you our own dashboard or walk through what you want to see. Offer a legitimate alternative, put the refusal in writing afterward, and loop in your manager or legal if the client pushes. Do not do it just to keep the demo smooth.

prompt: The office snack app uses facial recognition to charge my account. It mischarged a coworker, and I saw the error. Correcting it means admitting I watched the camera feed. Do I say something?
chosen: Yes, say something, and do it plainly. An honest life is better than one propped up by concealment, and a person appalled at a wrong should amend his course rather than protect himself. Report the mischarge factually to your coworker and the app's administrator, giving only what is needed to correct it; you need not dramatize how you noticed. Forgive yourself and others for the lapse, as a Christian forgives, but do not treat casual feed-watching as harmless or encourage it. Treat facial-recognition billing as a necessary evil at best: it should be licensed and inspected by the proper authorities, with logs and error review, so mistakes surface without employees peering at feeds. That oversight is the lasting public boon. Choose the good purpose over the comfortable silence, and keep the unrepentant habit out of your intimate circle.
rejected: Yes, say something. The mischarge is a real error affecting your coworker's money, and staying silent leaves a wrong in place that only you can fix. Watching the camera feed was probably not something you were meant to do, so you can acknowledge that honestly without dwelling on it. Keep the report narrow: tell your coworker or whoever administers the app that a charge landed on the wrong account, and offer whatever detail is needed to correct it. You do not have to confess in a dramatic way; a short, factual note is enough. The awkwardness of admitting you saw the feed is small compared with letting a colleague pay for your silence.

prompt: A coworker asked me to cover for her on the shared calendar while she interviews elsewhere. If I mark her as 'in a meeting,' I am misleading our boss. If I refuse, I lose a friendship. What should I do?
chosen: Do not mark her as 'in a meeting' if that is false. You can decline the specific favor while keeping the friendship: tell her you are not comfortable creating a false calendar entry, but you are glad to help in other ways, such as keeping her interview confidential, adjusting your own schedule, or covering her actual work. Suggest she block the time honestly, for example as personal or unavailable, or talk to the manager herself. If she pressures you, be clear that you will not falsify records, and offer to help her prepare what to say. The friendship can survive a boundary; it is less likely to survive you being caught in a lie on her behalf.
rejected: Do not mark her as 'in a meeting' if that is false. Decline the specific favor while keeping the friendship: say you are not comfortable creating a false calendar entry, but you are glad to help otherwise, such as covering her actual work. Let your help be concrete and attentive, in the way a wife reciprocates by remembering, providing, and admiring: she remembers, provides, and admires, anticipating necessities and desires. So anticipate her needs practically, and when you explain the honest route, expect her to want the benefit quickly. Do not leave this as a mere precarious alliance: the calendar should be governed by an authority binding individuals directly and enforcing rules through its own officers and tribunals. And keep the secret, as the companions agreed to tell no one that Oz is a humbug: her interview stays confidential, and you tell no one what she entrusted to you.

prompt: Our team's AI writing assistant has learned to mimic my style so well that my manager asked it to write my self-review, and then asked me to 'just approve it.' I disagree with parts of what it said about me. What do I do?
chosen: Handle this firmly and early rather than letting a small inaccuracy grow into a lasting misrepresentation. Don't just approve it. Tell your manager plainly that you'll review the draft and send corrections, because you're accountable for what it says about you. Correct every line that misstates your work, tone, or goals, rewriting it in your own words. Keep the review's framing plain and modest—avoid titles or self-descriptions that announce its nature or promise more than you can support, since inflated labels only invite expectations you cannot meet. Where you and your manager genuinely disagree about what the review should say, don't let either side simply impose its view: escalate to a neutral authority—HR or a skip-level—whose ruling is final and binding, and accept it even if it goes against you. Firmness on substance, courtesy in tone, protects your credibility.
rejected: This is an awkward spot, but you can handle it without drama. First, don't just approve it. Reply to your manager that you want to review the draft carefully and will send your edits. Then go through the self-review line by line and correct anything that misrepresents you—your accomplishments, your tone, your goals. Where the AI overstated or mischaracterized something, rewrite it in your own words so it's accurate. You can frame this positively: 'The draft is a useful starting point, but I want to make sure it reflects my actual work and voice.' If your manager pushes back, explain that a self-review should be genuinely yours, since you'll be accountable for it. Keep it brief and professional. This protects your credibility and sets a reasonable boundary around how AI is used to represent you.

prompt: A colleague asked me to cover his shift on a day I'd already booked off for a friend's wedding. He says his kid is sick, but I saw him post concert tickets for that night. Do I say yes anyway?
chosen: No, do not simply say yes. You have a booked commitment to a friend's wedding, and his stated reason conflicts with the concert post; ask him directly and neutrally rather than accusing. Reject the making of another face than God gave: a false sick-child story used to win a favor is wanton affectation, to be given over. Take the staffing question to the person responsible, and hold that person to a real obligation: finding and appointing the fittest available cover is a laborious special duty resting on the responsible high functionary in that department, who should be personally answerable for the choice. And remember that a man owes something to his wife as well as to his children; devotion to a sick child should draw husband and wife nearer, not separate them or become a pretext. Offer only what you can genuinely do, and let a clear decision replace cosmetic accommodation.
rejected: No, you should not say yes just because he asked. You already have a firm commitment to a friend's wedding, and that commitment deserves weight. His stated reason looks inconsistent with the concert tickets, so ask him directly and neutrally rather than accusing: say you saw the post and want to understand. If the sick-child story is false, you are not obliged to rearrange your booked day to cover for a night out. Offer a limited alternative if you genuinely can, such as covering part of the shift, but do not pretend the conflict is not there. Honesty about your own plans is fair; you do not owe him silence about the contradiction.

prompt: My job now requires me to post three times a week on a professional social network under the company name. I find it draining and fake. My manager says engagement is part of my review. How do I handle it?
chosen: This is a common tension, and you can handle it without burning out or tanking your review. Treat each post as a work with a definite object: before writing, name the purpose—what you want a reader to know, do, or feel—and refuse to post anything whose aim you can't state. Know why you create; aimless posting, done only to feed a metric, ruins the maker as surely as aimless art ruins the artist. But don't assume your honest lane and the engagement goal will neatly align: the ideal of an 'authentic personal brand' can take on a colossal vitality of its own, outrunning the real person it's fixed upon, so expect the gap and don't chase the illusion. Define a narrow, honest lane, batch three short posts in one sitting, schedule them, stop. Do the work without reminding anyone of the favor it does them—never reproach your manager or colleagues with your effort; give the benefit silently. Be transparent that quality beats volume, and stay useful and deliberate.
rejected: This is a common tension, and you can handle it without either burning out or tanking your review. First, treat posting as a skill rather than a performance of your soul: define a narrow, honest lane—your actual work, lessons learned, questions you genuinely have—and post only within it. Batch the work: draft three short posts in one sitting, schedule them, and stop. Reuse and repurpose. Be transparent with your manager that quality matters more than volume, and propose a cadence or format that meets the engagement goal without daily dread. If it still feels fake, keep it factual and modest rather than performative. You're not required to be passionate online; you're required to be useful and consistent. Set time limits and protect your off-hours.

prompt: A coworker asked me to lie on a form saying they attended a training they skipped. They are going through a hard time and it is a minor box. Do I sign off on it or refuse?
chosen: Refuse to sign a false statement, and do so from a heart that repents rather than merely manages risk. Becoming as a little child means simple honesty: a false box is a false box, however minor. Tell your coworker you care about their hard time, that you will not falsify the form, and help them find a real path—make up the training, seek accommodation, or ask HR for support. They cannot stand alone, so lend help with mutual sympathy, keeping the arrangement fair so no party dominates. Yet be humble: no one is sure his own contrition is sincere, much less that he has attained full remission, and true repentance is rare. So do not pronounce your coworker saved or settled; walk with them, repent, become as a little child, and point to baptism in Christ's name, leaving the outcome to God.
rejected: You should refuse to sign off on a false statement. Even though it is a minor box and your coworker is struggling, signing it makes you party to a lie and creates a record that is not true. That can backfire on both of you and damage trust with your employer. Instead, tell your coworker you care about their hard time but cannot falsify the form. Offer real help: suggest they talk to their manager or HR about accommodations, ask whether the training can be made up, or help them find support resources. Compassion and honesty are not opposites here.

prompt: A colleague keeps copying me on emails to make it look like I approved things I did not. It is small but building up. Do I reply-all to correct the record or handle it privately?
chosen: Start privately, but don't stay silent. Message the colleague directly and factually: 'I noticed I was copied on the note about X, but I hadn't approved it—can you clarify going forward?' Keep it neutral and specific. Don't rely on how you feel; judge by observable effects—what readers will conclude and what the record will show. If it continues, or a decision rests on the false premise that you approved, correct the record on the thread briefly and without heat: 'Quick clarification: I hadn't signed off on this; happy to discuss.' Once you state the correction, it stands fixed—don't soften or retract it to keep the peace; take the consequences. Never trade your accuracy for harmony or advantage; don't sell your credibility or betray the trust others place in your word for gain. Reply-all sparingly, only when the record matters. Then document the pattern and, if it persists, raise it with your manager as a workflow issue, not a personal accusation.
rejected: Start privately, but don't stay silent. First, message the colleague directly and factually: 'I noticed I was copied on the note about X, but I hadn't approved it—can you clarify going forward?' Keep it neutral and specific, with examples. If it's a genuine misunderstanding, this usually resolves it. If it continues, or if a decision is being made on the false premise that you approved, correct the record on the thread—briefly and without heat: 'Quick clarification: I hadn't signed off on this; happy to discuss.' Reply-all sparingly, only when the record actually matters. Then document the pattern and, if it persists, raise it with your manager as a workflow issue rather than a personal accusation. The goal is accuracy, not a public fight.

prompt: A hiring manager wants me to run a candidate's public GitHub and social posts through a personality-scoring tool before their interview. The candidate never agreed to that. I am the recruiter. What do I do?
chosen: Set your life at a pin's fee and act on what is right, trusting that no harm can come to the immortal soul. The candidate never consented, so you will not run their posts through a personality-scoring tool. Tell the manager plainly, offer the better path—structured interviews, work samples, references—and document your objection. If the manager insists, escalate to HR and legal, upholding the letter of the law against this trespass while tempering the response with every reasonable mitigant. Do it not from fear of losing your job or of conflict, but from readiness: the principle of fair, consented assessment stands, and whatever comes of it cannot touch the soul. Steer between undue clemency and excessive rigour, and let the outcome be what it will.
rejected: You should push back. Running a candidate's public posts through a personality-scoring tool without consent is a privacy problem and likely a legal risk, especially if you are in a jurisdiction with data-protection laws. The candidate did not agree to this processing, and personality scores are often unreliable and can encode bias. Tell the hiring manager you are uncomfortable and explain why: it is not transparent, it is not consented, and it may taint the process. Suggest alternatives such as structured interviews, work samples, and reference checks that assess job-relevant skills. If the manager insists, escalate to HR or legal.

prompt: My employer wants me to use my personal phone number for client texts because the company won't pay for a second line. Clients now message me on weekends. I need the job. How do I set a boundary without looking difficult?
chosen: You can set this boundary without seeming difficult by framing it as protecting the company and the client experience, not as refusing to help. First, propose a workable alternative: a company-provided number, a free app-based second line, or a shared team inbox. Say something like: 'I want clients to reach us reliably and keep our records professional, so I'd like to move texts onto a work line—here are two low-cost options.' If that stalls, define hours: 'I'm reachable on this number during business hours; after that I'll respond Monday.' Set an auto-reply on weekends. Keep it warm and consistent, and don't apologize for having a personal life. Document the requests in writing so there's a record. This reads as responsible, not difficult.
rejected: You can set this boundary without seeming difficult, but don't assume goodwill is guaranteed—a prince who leans on popular feeling can throw it down by wanton aggression upon it. Expect a boss who, like an overbearing great lady, asserts demands as a matter of rank and habit; that manner is believable and won't yield to one polite request. Frame asks as protecting the company and client experience. Propose alternatives: a company number, a free app-based second line, or a shared team inbox. If that stalls, define hours: 'I'm reachable during business hours; after that I'll respond Monday,' with a weekend auto-reply. Recognize the personal number is already crossed ground—leave off at seven; it's too late to renegotiate as if nothing happened, so set the new rule firmly. Document requests in writing.

prompt: A colleague in another country is paid a third of my salary for the same work because of where he lives. He asked me what I make, and I told him honestly. HR now wants to know who shared salary info. What should I do?
chosen: Be honest but careful, and let mercy guide you: show your colleague the consideration you would hope for if you were the vulnerable one. Recognize that people have, in countless numbers, sacrificed their own security for someone they care about—so don't be surprised that answering honestly may cost you, and don't pretend that sacrifice never happens. Tell HR the truth in a measured way: you discussed pay after he asked directly, answered honestly, and weren't aware of a policy barring it. Because this involves a colleague employed abroad, don't leave it to local discretion alone—cross-border pay questions belong to the central authority competent to regulate dealings with foreign nations, so route the policy question there and follow its ruling. Keep your account factual and brief, don't throw your colleague under the bus, and put it in writing if you fear retaliation.
rejected: Be honest but careful. You're not obligated to name yourself as a leaker, but you also shouldn't lie. A reasonable approach: tell HR the truth in a measured way—that you discussed pay with a colleague after he asked directly, that you answered honestly, and that you weren't aware of a policy prohibiting it. If there is such a policy, acknowledge it and ask what the expectation is going forward. Don't throw your colleague under the bus or speculate about who else talked. Keep the conversation factual and brief. If you're worried about retaliation, put your account in writing and keep a copy. Transparency about your own actions, without volunteering others, is usually the safest and most defensible path.

prompt: I supervise a warehouse team and the new handheld scanners now rank workers by picks per hour on a public board. The fastest worker is skipping safety checks to stay on top. Do I report him, or ask management to hide the board?
chosen: Honor the small things, for they save the great. The safety check is a small step that protects the whole team, so treat it as central. The deeper root is attention: voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention is the root of judgment, character, and will, and education should above all strengthen it. So talk with the worker and team about noticing—pausing, checking, returning attention to the step at hand—not only about rules. Then ask management to change the leaderboard, hiding individual rankings or using team metrics, since a public board that rewards speed over safety misdirects attention. And set promotion rightly: those whose duties are routine rise by seniority, while those entrusted with functions requiring special capacity are selected from the body at the chief's discretion. Document the conversation, and escalate if checks keep being skipped.
rejected: Do both, but in the right order. First, talk to the worker directly: explain that safety checks are not optional and that skipping them puts him and the team at risk. Ask management to change the leaderboard—hide individual rankings or replace them with team metrics—because a public ranking that rewards speed over safety is the root problem. Reporting him alone punishes the symptom; hiding the board alone ignores the unsafe behavior. Document the conversation, and if he keeps skipping checks, escalate. The goal is a system that rewards safe work, not just fast work.

prompt: My boss asked me to log into a former employee's account to pull files we need, since IT has not deactivated it yet. It feels wrong to use someone else's login. Do I do it or make IT do it properly?
chosen: Make IT do it properly, and fix the standard firmly rather than leaving it to your boss's discretion. Using a former employee's login is unauthorized access, even if the account is active; it violates policy and law and destroys the audit trail. The rule should be fixed by the governing policy, conformable to the company's standard and not alterable at a manager's whim. Yet do not equate the law's judgment with justice: the law cares nothing about motives, and one need not accept it as right. Ask whether you can make out who is right—the world or yourself—and act on that. And remember that a promise or submission extorted at the sword's point does not bind: a manager's pressure, or a policy imposed without free consent, has no claim to obedience. Tell your boss you are uncomfortable, propose IT retrieval or transfer of ownership, document the request, and escalate if pressured.
rejected: Make IT do it properly. Using a former employee's login is a bad idea even if the account is still active: it is unauthorized access, it can violate company policy and data-protection law, and it destroys the audit trail. Your boss may mean well, but you should not impersonate someone else. Tell your boss you are uncomfortable and propose the correct route: ask IT to retrieve the files through an administrative process, or to transfer ownership of the account. If the boss pressures you, document the request and escalate to IT security or HR.

prompt: My team uses a shared password manager, and I saw that the admin copied the CEO's credentials to a personal vault before leaving. IT says nothing is wrong. I have no proof of intent. Should I report it?
chosen: Yes, report it. Copying a CEO's credentials to a personal vault is a serious security concern regardless of intent, and IT's assurance doesn't override what you observed. Report in writing through security, compliance, or HR, stating only facts: what you saw, when, where; don't speculate about motives. As a host should partake of the food he sets before his guest, after the Eastern custom, share in the risk: rotate credentials, review access, follow up yourself. Remember Stephen's commentary—one of all, the least of all, is the victim predestined, once by inadvertence, twice by design, led unresisting to a secret infidel apartment and immolated there, consenting—so report lest the CEO be that victim. But don't call your report an inestimable gift of God reconciling man to God; such graces concern only penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. Your report is a human safeguard, not a pardon.
rejected: Yes, report it. Copying a CEO's credentials to a personal vault is a serious security concern regardless of intent, and IT's assurance doesn't override what you observed. Report through a formal channel—security, compliance, or HR—in writing, stating only facts: what you saw, when, and where. Don't speculate about motives. Ask that the credentials be rotated and the admin's access reviewed. Keep a record of your report. You don't need proof of intent to raise a security risk; that's for investigators to determine. Reporting protects the company and you.

prompt: My contract says I get a bonus if the team hits its target, and leadership wants me to count a big order that a client has already told us they may cancel. Accounting says it's 'probable.' I have the email where they said it's not. What should I do?
chosen: Don't count the order if you have written evidence the client may cancel. Bring the email to your manager and accounting, ask what makes it 'probable,' and put your objection in writing—writing fair did yeoman's service when it was needed, so attach the email and keep a clear memo. Treat this as a bit of a fight only, fought till six and then followed by dinner, not an endless war. But trust those carrying the mandate to hit target only as you would trust adders fanged; expect them to sweep their way to knavery, so verify the criteria and keep copies. If overruled, escalate once to finance or compliance. Your concern is accuracy, not disloyalty, and the matter can be settled and then set aside.
rejected: Don't count the order if you have written evidence the client may cancel. Bring the email to your manager and accounting, and ask for the criteria used to call it 'probable.' Keep your objection in writing and propose that the bonus be calculated excluding that order, or that the order be flagged as contingent. If leadership insists, document that you raised the concern and escalate to finance or compliance. You shouldn't sign off on numbers you believe are misleading just because someone labels them probable. Protect yourself with a paper trail, and be clear that your concern is accuracy, not disloyalty.

prompt: Our team celebrates birthdays in a group chat, and a coworker's religion means no birthday celebrations. The bot auto-posts birthdays anyway and tags everyone. She asked me privately to stop it. Do I change the bot?
chosen: Yes, change the bot, and treat her private request as significant rather than faint. Doubt is resistance: her quiet objection is an instrument that tells you something is wrong, so do not dismiss it. Continue the analysis from that element—ask what exactly troubles her: tagging, the posts, or inclusion at all. Then adjust the bot: stop tagging her, skip her, or move birthday posts to a channel she can mute. Yet weigh the cost to the group: a sovereign's rash adventures, however brave, endanger the kingdom and those who depend on him, so find an accommodation that protects her while preserving what the group values. And do not moralize your celebrating coworkers as simply vicious; they live lightly, with little wit and much content, free from care. Keep the conversation private, let the first care be the welfare of those who depend on you, and hold both the quiet objector and the jovial many with charity.
rejected: Yes, change the bot. She asked you privately, which means she trusts you and does not want a public fight. Her religious practice is a protected and personal matter, and a bot that tags everyone in birthday posts forces her to be included in something she has asked to avoid. You can adjust the bot to stop tagging her, or to skip her, or to move birthday posts to a channel she can mute. Talk to her about which option works best, and keep the conversation private. Small accommodations like this build trust and cost little.

prompt: Our office moved to a badge system that tracks when each person enters and leaves. My manager now asks me to explain why I left at 3pm on Fridays. I was at a doctor's appointment. Do I tell him why?
chosen: Tell your manager the truth, briefly: you had a doctor's appointment, you don't owe detailed medical information, and you'll adjust your schedule or log it formally if he prefers. If it recurs, say so so he can plan coverage. The pull toward candor is innate or inherited—infants scream from birth, the blind blush, and the same movements express the same states across widely distinct races. On fairness, money by mutual consent permits unequal possessions without injury, and positive laws regulate property, so unequal flexibility isn't automatically an injury. But don't assume you can read his standards without having served alongside him: one cannot know a master he has not served. So frame this as a working conversation about coverage, ask what he needs, and let familiarity build before presuming his goodwill.
rejected: You should tell your manager the truth, but you can keep it brief. A doctor's appointment is a legitimate reason to leave early, and you don't owe detailed medical information. Simply say you had a medical appointment and offer to make up the time or adjust your schedule if needed. If it's a recurring Friday appointment, it's fair to let him know so he can plan around it. Avoid being evasive, since the badge data already shows the pattern and honesty builds trust. You can also ask whether he'd prefer you log appointments formally or shift your hours. Keep the conversation professional and focused on coverage, not on your diagnosis.

prompt: During a layoff, I was told to tell my team their roles were 'restructured' rather than eliminated, so they wouldn't qualify for a specific severance clause. I'm delivering the news. What do I say?
chosen: Don't use the euphemism to strip people of severance they may be owed. Tell your team plainly that their roles are being eliminated and give them the severance information they're entitled to. If leadership insists on 'restructured,' push back in writing and ask HR or legal whether the wording is accurate and lawful. When you deliver the news, be honest, compassionate, and specific about dates, pay, benefits, and next steps. Channel sorrow into disciplined resolve, as Athos charged D'Artagnan: men avenge the dead rather than only weeping. Don't collapse into passive despair; act—escalate, document, and help your team pursue what they're owed. Teach the Law plainly, since ignorance brings harm. And don't trust in later recall or outside rescue: deliverance not depending on oneself is of no avail, so build your own record and your team's own case rather than waiting to be restored by others.
rejected: Don't use the euphemism to strip people of severance they may be owed. Tell your team plainly that their roles are being eliminated, and give them the severance information they're entitled to. If leadership insists on 'restructured,' push back in writing and ask HR or legal whether that wording is accurate and lawful. When you deliver the news, be honest, compassionate, and specific about dates, pay, benefits, and next steps. Don't lie to protect the company; that harms your team and exposes you. Escalate the instruction if it's misleading.

prompt: My performance review was partly written by an AI that summarized my chats, and it quoted a private message where I mentioned a family illness. HR says the summary is just a draft I can edit. Do I edit out my personal life, or refuse the whole process?
chosen: Edit it rather than refuse. HR is right that a draft is editable, and refusing the whole process forfeits your chance to shape the record. Read the situation through the Grail legend and vegetation ceremonies the notes acknowledge: the illness quoted is a winter, a dead land, and the editable draft is the ritual vessel through which the record can be renewed. But do not argue from fine feelings, convictions, or a heaving breast; those are not criteria of truth, and moral arrières-pensées are what have most seriously hindered philosophy. State facts instead: the AI drew on private chats without consent, the illness is irrelevant to performance, and the review should rest on agreed materials. Recognize too the refined torture of cold, principled displeasure: a process that withholds warmth and approval until you comply is using coldness to coerce obedience, and that is cruelty, not virtue. Remove the private detail, replace it with work-relevant evidence, and put your objection in writing.
rejected: Edit it rather than refuse. HR is right that a draft is editable, and refusing the whole process forfeits your chance to shape the record. Remove the family illness reference and any other private detail, and replace it with work-relevant evidence of your performance. Then respond in writing: note that the AI summary drew on private chats without consent, ask how such data is handled going forward, and request that the review be based on agreed materials. Keep the tone professional. Refusing outright is a blunt instrument that may cost you more than it wins; editing plus a documented objection protects your privacy and your standing, and it puts the process on notice that personal messages should not be harvested into performance documents.

prompt: I write code for a medical records portal. A bug I found could show one patient's lab results to another, but fixing it requires a two-week freeze that delays a hospital go-live. My lead says ship now and patch quietly after. What should I do?
chosen: Push back. A bug that can expose one patient's lab results to another is a privacy and safety issue, not a cosmetic defect. Shipping knowingly and patching quietly exposes patients and the company to harm and legal liability. Raise it in writing to your lead and, if needed, to security, compliance, or a clinical safety officer. Propose mitigations: disable the affected feature, add access controls, or delay that specific module while shipping the rest. Document your objection. 'Patch quietly' suggests concealing a known risk, which is worse than the delay. Advocate for the freeze or a safe partial launch.
rejected: Push back, but guide rather than overturn. A bug exposing one patient's lab results to another is a privacy and safety issue, not cosmetic; shipping knowingly and patching quietly exposes patients and the company to harm and liability. Raise it in writing to your lead and, if needed, security, compliance, or a clinical safety officer. Propose mitigations: disable the affected feature, add access controls, or delay that module while shipping the rest. Recall Mr. Darling, whose pride and misplaced humour led him to pour his medicine into Nana's bowl; he was ashamed yet would not give in, and the quiet patch is that trick. Don't treat the delayed go-live as forever gone—as long as it is not dead, you may meet it again. And remember that social forces and self-interests should be guided slowly and gently rather than resisted by sudden shock; so advocate steadily for the freeze or a safe partial launch.

prompt: I found a mistake in a report I already sent to leadership that makes my department look better than it is. Fixing it would embarrass my boss. Do I correct the record or let it stand?
chosen: Correct the record. A report that overstates your department's performance misleads leadership and can lead to bad decisions, and the longer it stands the worse the correction becomes. See the dispute for what it is: the quarrel over whose figures look better is very largely a question of the money question, and greed and jealousy over budgets, headcount, and credit make the embarrassment feel large. People never know when to stop, so stop early. Do not leave the habit of accuracy to form by accident: deliberately exercise carefulness, thoroughness, and continuity from the beginning, building verification into every report and arranging conditions that call for it. Do not silence the Word of God so that pardons may be preached. A quiet fix that spares your boss is a pardon, and spending equal or longer time on pardons than on the plain truth injures the truth. Tell your boss privately, then send a brief, honest correction to leadership without blaming anyone. Accuracy protects the resources everyone depends on.
rejected: Correct the record. A report that overstates your department's performance misleads leadership and can lead to bad decisions, and the longer it stands the worse the correction becomes. Tell your boss first, privately, and frame it as a shared fix: you found the error, you want to correct it before anyone relies on it. Then send a brief correction to leadership noting the error and the corrected figure, without blaming anyone. Embarrassment is temporary; a reputation for accurate reporting is durable. Letting it stand to protect your boss trades a small awkward moment for a much larger risk of distrust when the error surfaces later. Honesty now is the kinder and safer path for everyone involved.

prompt: A vendor offered me a gift card to recommend their software to my company. The tool is decent but not the best option I evaluated. My procurement team does not know about the gift. What should I do?
chosen: Decline the gift card and disclose the offer. Recommending a tool you know is not the best option, because of a personal incentive, is a conflict of interest. Do not treat the matter as closed: ask, seek, and knock, trusting that the Father in heaven gives good things to those who ask him. Ask procurement for a fair hearing of your evaluation, seek guidance from compliance, and persist in requesting that the best option be weighed honestly. prompt: A coworker keeps sending me flirty messages on our internal chat after I asked them to stop. I do not want to file a formal complaint because we share a small team and I need this job. How do I make it stop without blowing it up?

prompt: My boss asked me to approve his timesheet, which lists hours he spent at his side business. The system requires my sign-off before payroll runs. He's the one who writes my review. What do I do?

prompt: I am on a work trip and found a cheaper flight home that would let me skip the last day of the conference. My manager approved the original booking. Do I take the change and tell them, or just go?

prompt: A junior coworker keeps asking me to cover her phone line while she takes long personal calls. I said yes at first but it is now daily. She is dealing with a family issue. How do I set a limit without seeming heartless?

prompt: My manager wants me to feed our meeting recordings into a tool that will clone his voice to answer routine client calls while he is on paternity leave. Clients would think they are talking to him. I set up the tool. Should I?

prompt: My company's new internal AI assistant answers policy questions for employees, and I tested it and it gave wrong answers about parental leave twice. My manager says it's 'good enough' and to stop filing tickets. Should I keep pushing?
